title: The French Way
subtitle: A Pilgrim's Guide to the Camino Francés
author: CaminoPlus

spans.t: The French Way is the most walked of the Caminos. It begins in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, a small town in the French Pyrenees, and ends at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, in Galicia. The CaminoPlus catalog gives it as ~773 km, walked in 33 usual stages. That is about a month of walking, and more with rest days.
The promise of this book is simple.
By the last page you will know whether this is your Camino, where to start and how long to give it, when to go, what to carry, and what each of the 33 days asks of you.
How to use it
If you are a month or more away, read the chapters in order up to "Before you go". Then read the five regional chapters, which hold the days, and the chapters that follow them.

If you are on the road tonight, go straight to your stage. Each day says what the walking is like, what is worth a pause and where to take care. Where a day has its own stage in the CaminoPlus app today, its entry ends with a pointer. Not every day does yet.
If you are only dreaming, read "Is this Camino for you?", then "The inner Way". The rest can wait.
What this book is not
This book was written with AI assistance, from public sources, and its author has not walked the road. So it gives you sources instead of memories, and it says plainly when the sources disagree.

It is not a live map, a timetable or a booking service. It names no hostels, cafes or shops, and it gives no prices, opening hours or bed counts, because they change from season to season and a wrong one costs a tired person dearly. For those, use the CaminoPlus app and ask locally.
Every distance carries a tilde,

, because it is approximate. Published stage lengths differ from one source to the next, by a kilometre or two and sometimes more, and the book says so where it matters. Where something depends on the season (a closure, a diversion, snow, heat), it says
check before you go
, and means it.
A few words you will meet
Buen Camino
, "good Way", is what pilgrims and locals say to one another as you pass. An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel. The
credencial
is your pilgrim's passport, a folded card that you carry and have stamped along the way; each stamp is a
sello
. The
Compostela
is the certificate that the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago gives to those who meet its rules, which you will meet in plain words in the chapter on where to start.
They are explained again when they first matter, and used plainly after that.
Pack lightly, start slowly, and take your time over the long hill.
Buen Camino.
The route
The French Way, the
Camino Francés

, starts in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port, whose name means "Saint John at the foot of the pass". It was the old capital of the Basque province of Lower Navarre, and Wikipedia calls it the second most popular start of the French Way. From there the road crosses the Pyrenees to Roncesvalles, then runs west through Pamplona, Logroño, Burgos and León to Santiago de Compostela.

The catalog gives the length as ~773 km. Published figures run from about 770 to about 780: Wikipedia's example itinerary starts at ~769 km from Santiago, German Wikipedia quotes the cathedral's pilgrim portal at ~774 km, and the 33 stage figures in this book add up to ~777 km. Which is right depends on where you measure from and which variant you walk, so treat ~775 km as a good guide.
Wikipedia says a typical walk takes at least four weeks, with one or two rest days. This book follows 33 usual stage towns, an average of ~24 km a day.
Where the road comes from

Three routes across France (from Tours, Vézelay and Le Puy-en-Velay) meet at Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. A fourth, the Aragonese Way, crosses the Pyrenees at Somport and joins the French Way at Puente la Reina, ~690 km from Santiago. Later the Camino Primitivo joins at Melide and the Camino del Norte at Arzúa.
A short history

The Xunta de Galicia, the regional government, gives this account on its official portal. Around the year 820 the tomb of St James the Elder was found in a wood called Libredón, and King Alfonso II of Asturias ordered a church built there. That church was the seed of the cathedral and the city. Asturian kings were among the first known pilgrims, and by the 11th to 13th centuries people were arriving from France, Italy, Germany, England and beyond, on foot, on horseback and by ship. A network of hospitals founded by kings, nobles and townspeople took them in, and in the small medieval ones it was customary to keep twelve beds, in memory of the twelve apostles.
The road got its name from the settlers. German Wikipedia says the name
Camino Francés
is first recorded in the 12th century, at Astorga, and refers to the French settlers whom the kings of northern Spain invited to build market towns along it.
Book V of the
Codex Calixtinus

is a medieval guide to this road, covering its stages, sanctuaries, hospitality, fountains and food. It is often attributed to the French cleric Aymeric Picaud. The Xunta dates the codex to 1135; Wikipedia says about 1138 to 1145, and calls the attribution to Picaud likely rather than certain.

The pilgrimage never stopped, but it thinned. The Reformation, the wars of religion and the French Revolution cut the numbers, and in 1589, fearing an English attack, the archbishop of Santiago had the apostle's remains hidden; they were found again in 1879. The recovery of the road began in the 20th century. The Xunta names the first modern associations of friends of the Camino, founded in Paris in 1950 and in Estella in 1963, and the visit of Pope John Paul II in 1982. UNESCO inscribed the Camino Francés on the World Heritage List in 1993.
The Way today

In 2024 the Pilgrim's Office issued 499,239 Compostelas, and 47 per cent of them went to people who walked the French Way, according to Wikipedia: about 235,000 people. Of those, about 14 per cent started in Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port. About 65 per cent started in Sarria, the town ~115 km from Santiago, which the chapter on where to start explains.
What it feels like
The road changes character five times, and this book is built on that.

items.t: A steep start, then green hills, Pamplona and the rolling country beyond.
A great cathedral, then the high plateau, at ~800 to ~900 m, for days.
A great city, then the mountains: the road passes ~1,500 m at the Cruz de Ferro, its highest point.
O Cebreiro, at ~1,300 m, is the gateway. From there to Santiago the Xunta measures ~155 km through a greener, wetter country.

spans.t: People walk this road for many reasons. It is long enough to ask something of you, and the villages along it have been receiving pilgrims for more than a thousand years.
Long, not technical

The French Way asks for time and stamina more than skill. It is a walking path, and most of the distance is on tracks, field edges and village streets. The Xunta de Galicia rates the Galician section "Medium", and its stages run from "Low" to "Medium-High". The days in this book run from ~18 to ~30 km. What makes the Francés demanding is the number of them: 33 in a row, with a rest day or two on top.

A fair test comes from the Confraternity of St James: aim to be able to walk ~20 km or more a day, over varied ground, with your pack on. If you can do that on a training weekend, you are ready to start slowly. The Confraternity adds that you will get fitter by walking the Camino itself.
The days that ask the most
A few days are harder than the rest, and it is better to know them now. The figures are worked out from altitudes in Wikipedia's route tables, so read them as ~ guides.

items.t: A net climb of ~1,250 m, from ~175 m to ~1,430 m, before the drop to Roncesvalles.
Day 24, down from the Cruz de Ferro.
About ~850 m of descent in ~19 km, hard on knees.
A net climb of ~800 m over ~30 km.
Not steep, but open, and in summer hot. Day 17 passes ~17 to ~18 km without a village.

spans.t: Who it suits

items.t: who want a path with a long tradition and plenty of company. It is the most walked of the Caminos: in 2024, 47 per cent of Compostelas went to people on the French Way, against 19 per cent for the Portuguese Way, the next most walked.
and a wish to see Spain change by the day: Basque hills, vineyards, a plateau, mountains, green Galicia.
People who like cities in the middle of a walk.
Pamplona, Logroño, Burgos and León make natural pauses.

spans.t: Who might choose another

items.t: If you have a week or two,

do not squeeze the whole Francés into it. Start later (the next chapter shows where), or choose a shorter Camino. In the app's catalog the Portuguese Way from Porto is ~240 km, the English Way ~120 km and the walk to Finisterre and Muxía ~90 km.
If you want a quiet road,

the Francés in high season is not it, especially after Sarria. Choose another season, another Camino, or start where fewer people do. Of the people who walked the Francés in 2024, about 65 per cent started in Sarria.
look at the Coastal and Northern Ways. The Northern Way is ~820 km, according to the catalog.
If heat or a long month away worries you,
read "When to go" and "Body, weather and safety" before you decide. A shorter walk, in a milder month, is a real Camino too.

spans.t: Every reason is a good reason

People walk for faith, for sport, for grief, to think, to stop thinking, because a friend did, or because a calendar had a gap. At the end of the walk the Pilgrim's Office asks about your motivation, as the chapter on arriving explains. Its credencial is, in the Office's own words, for those who walk with a Christian sentiment, "even if it is only with an attitude of search". The chapter on the inner Way says more.

chapters.title: Where to start, and how many days

spans.t: You can begin almost anywhere

Nobody has to walk all 33 stages. The road is the same road from every town on it, and it can be walked in pieces over several years. This list shows how far each usual start is from Santiago, and how many of this book's days follow it. The figures are worked out from the stage figures in this book, so they are ~ guides. Other tables differ by several kilometres over such distances: Wikipedia's example itinerary puts Pamplona ~700 km from Santiago, where Spanish Wikipedia has ~712 km.

items.t: ~777 km, 33 days. The whole Way, and the steepest first day.
~712 km, 30 days. A city start that skips the Pyrenees.
~491 km, 21 days. The Meseta, the mountains and Galicia.
~312 km, 13 days. About a fortnight, with the mountains and Galicia.
~115 km, 5 days. By far the most common start in 2024.

spans.t: Wikipedia says that a typical walk of the whole road takes at least four weeks, with a rest day or two. Pamplona, Burgos and León are the three natural places for one, and a quiet day after the Pyrenees is a kindness to your legs.
Sample plans
These are sums, not prescriptions, worked out from the stage figures.

items.t: The whole road in about five weeks:
33 walking days, rest days at Pamplona (after day 3), Burgos (after day 12) and León (after day 20), and a last day in Santiago: 37 days.
21 walking days, three weeks, and a rest day in León makes 22.
13 walking days, so about a fortnight with one rest day.
5 walking days, plus a day in Santiago.

spans.t: The Compostela, in the Office's words

The Compostela is the certificate issued by the Pilgrim's Office in Santiago. The Office says it is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons and follow the routes of the Way of St James on foot, by bicycle or on horseback.

On foot or on horseback, the Office asks for at least the last hundred kilometres, and by bicycle the last two hundred, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route. On foot or on horseback that means at least a hundred continuous kilometres on the same route to Santiago that the Office recognises, and the final stage must include at least the last one leading into the Cathedral.

The Way may be done in stages, if they follow one another in chronological and geographical order. A pilgrim who walks only the minimum distance must get the credencial stamped at the start and the end of each stage, with the date. A pilgrim who has already walked part of a recognised route outside Spain needs no less than seventy kilometres in Spain. The Cabildo, the cathedral's governing council, reserves the right to grant the Compostela in special and exceptional cases.
What that means on this road

The French Way is long, so most starts are far above the limit. Sarria is the usual place to begin the last stretch, and sources put it between ~108 and ~115 km from the cathedral: Wikipedia's example itinerary gives ~108 km, Spanish Wikipedia ~113 km, Wikipedia's article on Sarria ~115 km, and the Xunta de Galicia's own stages from Sarria add up to ~115 km. Every one of those figures is more than a hundred kilometres. One stage later, Portomarín is ~93 km away by the Xunta's figures, which is less. Published figures differ, and the Office decides, not this book, so if your plan is close to the limit, or unusual, ask the Pilgrim's Office before you go.
Splitting the days

The stage towns in this book are the usual ones, not the only ones. The longest days, 7, 8, 26 and 31, are each ~28 to ~30 km, and day 17, with ~17 to ~18 km between villages, is better planned with food and water in mind. Wikipedia's example itinerary splits the road differently in several places, for example at Rabanal del Camino, ~20 km after Astorga, or at Calzadilla de la Cueza, ~17 km after Carrión. Choose the plan that suits your legs, and look at the app for where to sleep.

The French Way crosses mountains, a high plateau and the green hills of Galicia, so "the weather" is several weathers. No month is perfect along all of it. What follows are patterns, not forecasts. Before any day, look at the local weather.
How many people, and when
Most pilgrims finish between May and September, says Wikipedia. Its chart of the Pilgrim's Office figures for 2024 shows how steep the seasons are on this road:
The monthly figures add up to less than the year's total of "over 235,000" that the same article gives, so read them as a shape, not a count.
What the seasons are like
The temperatures below are monthly averages for 1991 to 2020, as listed on Wikipedia (the figures for Burgos and Santiago come from the Spanish weather service). Extremes are far wider than averages.
Spring (March to June).
Quiet in March, busy by May. In Burgos, at ~865 m, the average June day reaches ~24 °C. Early in the season, ask about conditions on the Pyrenees and the high ground of León and Galicia.
Summer (July and August).

Hot, and on the Meseta exposed. The average July high is ~28 °C in both Pamplona and Burgos; the records are ~42 °C in Pamplona and ~39 °C in Burgos. Galicia is cooler (the average July high in Santiago is ~25 °C) and much drier than in winter. In Pamplona the San Fermín festival runs from 6 to 14 July, and the city fills.
Autumn (September and October).
The crowds thin by October and the days shorten. The rain also returns: Santiago averages ~89 mm in September and ~214 mm in October.
Winter (November to February).

Few walkers, short days and cold. In Burgos the average January day reaches only ~7 °C and the average night falls to about freezing; the record low is about 22 degrees below freezing. In Santiago the average January day is ~12 °C, and the month brings ~196 mm of rain. The high route over the Pyrenees is closed to walkers in winter; in November 2025 Navarre's government announced a closure from 1 November to 31 March, so check the notice for your year. Many places that serve pilgrims in summer may be shut, so ask before you rely on one.
Rain, heat and light

Santiago receives ~1,500 mm of rain a year, against ~720 mm in Pamplona and ~550 mm in Burgos. The Xunta de Galicia advises a waterproof garment whatever the season, and a cap against the sun, and against cold in the high places.

Daylight changes more than people expect. Anywhere on the road, the day lasts ~9 hours at the December solstice and ~15 hours at the June solstice, by a standard solar calculation. In December the sun rises between about half past eight in Saint-Jean and nine in Santiago, so a winter walker has little time to waste.
Holy Years

A Jacobean Holy Year occurs when 25 July, the feast of St James, falls on a Sunday. The next one is 2027, then 2032. The Confraternity of St James says Holy Years bring a huge surge in pilgrims, and that Santiago becomes extremely busy, particularly around Easter and the feast of St James. It recommends booking accommodation as far ahead as you can.
Choosing

If you want company and warm days, May, June and September suit most people. If you want fewer people, April and October are quieter, and you should carry a coat. If you must walk in July or August, start early every day and plan for the Meseta's heat.
Check before you go:
the route over the Pyrenees, snow and fog on the high stages, heat warnings, and wildfires.
The credencial
The
credencial

is your pilgrim's passport, and you need it for two things: to sleep in pilgrims' hostels, and to prove your walk when you ask for the Compostela. The Pilgrim's Office describes the official model as a card of sixteen concertina-folded pages. The first page holds your details, and the rest hold boxes for stamps. Each stamp is a
sello

You can get one from the Pilgrim's Reception Office in Santiago, from confraternities and associations of friends of the Way that the Cathedral has authorised, from parish churches and from pilgrim hostels. The Office keeps a list for your country. Get yours before you leave if you can.

Stamps are normally collected where you sleep, and also in parish churches, monasteries, cathedrals, hotels, town halls and other places. The Office also describes a digital credential for phones. For the Compostela it speaks of the stamped credencial, so carry the paper one, and ask the Office if you want to rely on anything else.
Getting there, and back
Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port is in France. A regional train, the TER, runs from Bayonne, along a line ~52 km long, according to Wikipedia. Timetables and connections change, so check them before you book.

Santiago has its own airport, Santiago-Rosalía de Castro, ~12 km from the city, with flights to Spanish and other European cities. Leave a spare day or two at the end: the walk finishes where you can rest, and the Compostela queue can be long.
Training

The Confraternity of St James suggests that, if you are not an experienced walker, you walk regularly, add longer distances and hills as you improve, and aim to be able to cover ~20 km or more a day on varied ground. It also advises:

items.t: Break in new boots or shoes and socks before you go.
Practise with your loaded rucksack, because a pack changes the way your feet strike the ground, and with poles, if you will use them.
Train for the downhill too. This matters on the Francés: the descent from the Cruz de Ferro, ~850 m in ~19 km, is one of the biggest of the walk.
Take rest days in your training, and stretch before and after.

spans.t: The Xunta de Galicia says to start training some months ahead, with walks that grow gradually longer, up to training walks of ~23 to ~30 km. If you have a medical condition or any worry, speak to a doctor or physiotherapist first.
Packing

Carry less than you think. The Confraternity notes that some people advise no more than 10 to 15 per cent of your body weight, counting the day's food and water: a litre of water weighs a kilogram. It suggests a base weight, without food and water but with the rucksack, of ~7 to ~10 kg, and a rucksack of 35 to 60 litres. Weigh your pack at home.

The Xunta's list of basics includes boots and light shoes for the evening, seamless socks, two T-shirts and two jerseys, a sleeping bag, a canteen, high-factor sunscreen, a hat or cap, a small first-aid kit, a phone and charger, and a waterproof garment in every season. Earplugs and a torch are among its optional extras. Add little to that list: a lighter pack is the better advice.

Three notes. The Confraternity says that a reflective vest is a legal requirement in Spain when you walk on roads in darkness or poor visibility, and a good idea in hunting season. Poles and a stick are a matter of taste, and most airlines will not let you carry a stick in the cabin. And the weather you meet may be anything from cold rain to ~40 °C, so pack for the month you will walk.
Shoes and feet

The Xunta advises a hard sole and a heel that is not too soft, and comfortable shoes broken in beforehand. The Confraternity suggests boots in winter, late autumn, early spring, on very rough ground or if you have ankle problems, notes that some people dislike Gore-Tex boots in hot dusty weather, and advises buying from a specialist shop that will let you try them at home. Do not buy boots that do not quite fit just because the price is low. Foot cream, seamless cotton socks and footwear that has been broken in are the Xunta's advice for keeping your feet healthy.
Money, phone and language
The Xunta advises carrying your documents and cards and not much cash. Spain uses the euro. Keep a little cash for small places that may not take cards, and ask in the app where you are.
Charge your phone every evening. CaminoPlus is built to work without signal, so check in the app that the maps you need are on your phone before you leave home.

Spanish is the language of the road, and Galician is also an official language in Galicia. Place names appear in more than one form: Roncesvalles is also Orreaga in Basque, Pamplona is also Iruña, and Palas de Rei is also written Palas de Rey. A few Spanish words,
por favor
gracias
and
buenos días
, go a long way.
Health and booking

See a doctor if you have any condition that the walk could affect, and check that your insurance covers you in Spain. In May to September, and in a Holy Year, book beds ahead where you can. The Confraternity says so for Holy Years in particular.
The character of these days

The first week begins with the biggest climb of the walk and settles into green hills, Pamplona and the rolling country beyond. Navarre is a land of two languages: Roncesvalles is also Orreaga in Basque, and Pamplona is Iruña. It has fine Romanesque churches, at Eunate and Torres del Río among other places.

The distances in this book are rounded. For days 1 to 3 they come from the CaminoPlus stage data, and from day 4 on from public tables, chiefly Wikipedia's example itinerary and the Xunta de Galicia (see "Sources"). Tables differ by a kilometre or two, and the days say so where the gap is bigger. Many pilgrims split days differently; this book follows the usual stage towns.
Day 1: Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port to Roncesvalles (~24 km)

The hardest day comes first. Saint-Jean sits at ~175 m, the road climbs to the Lepoeder pass at ~1,430 m, and then it drops to Roncesvalles at ~950 m. That is a net climb of ~1,250 m, with the border crossing on the way.

There are two routes. The high one over Lepoeder is closed to walkers in winter (Navarre's government announced a closure from 1 November to 31 March in November 2025). The lower road by Valcarlos and the Ibañeta pass, at ~1,057 m, is the way in bad weather and in winter. Check the notice for your year.

Roncesvalles is a village below the pass where, in 778, the Basques ambushed the rearguard of Charlemagne's army, the battle behind the legend of Roland. Go slowly, carry food and water for the climb, and remember that this day is not the whole walk.
In the app: stage 1.
Day 2: Roncesvalles to Zubiri (~21 km)
A gentler day, mostly downhill, with a pass or two in the middle. You pass through Burguete and Espinal, over the Mezkiritz pass at ~925 m and the Erro pass at ~800 m, and drop to Zubiri, at ~530 m.
The thing to watch is the end. The last ~6 km fall ~270 m, steep enough to find out how your knees feel. Poles help, and so does taking it slowly.
In the app: stage 2.
Day 3: Zubiri to Pamplona (~20 km)
The path runs through Larrasoaña, Zuriáin and Zabaldika, then the towns of Villava and Burlada, and into Pamplona, at ~450 m. Sources give this stage as ~20 to ~22 km.

Pamplona's old walls and the Portal de Francia, the gate pilgrims from France entered by, are worth a look as you arrive. The cathedral is 15th-century Gothic, with a 13th- and 14th-century cloister. The San Fermín festival runs from 6 to 14 July, and the city is then very busy. At other times it makes a good first rest day.
In the app: stage 3.
Day 4: Pamplona to Puente la Reina (~24 km)

The day's climb is the Alto del Perdón, at ~765 m, on the Sierra del Perdón ridge, where a sculpture of iron pilgrims by Vicente Galbete, put up in 1996, stands against the sky. The descent is steep: ~285 m in ~4 km down to Uterga.

If you have energy, a detour of ~2 km from Muruzábal leads to Santa María de Eunate, an octagonal 12th-century Romanesque church standing alone in open country. Puente la Reina, "the Queen's bridge", is where the Aragonese Way joins.
Day 5: Puente la Reina to Estella (~22 km)

A rolling day between ~345 m and ~500 m, through hill villages: Mañeru, Cirauqui, Lorca and Villatuerta. Estella was founded in 1090, by a charter from King Sancho Ramírez, and became a landmark of the pilgrim road. Its Romanesque buildings include the church of San Pedro de la Rúa and the Palace of the Kings of Navarre.
The Xunta names Estella, in 1963, as one of the two places where the first modern associations of friends of the Camino were founded, the start of the road's revival. The other was Paris, in 1950.
Day 6: Estella to Los Arcos (~22 km)

You pass Ayegui and the Monastery of Irache, a former Benedictine monastery whose origins go back to the 8th century, though the surviving buildings are later. Then come Azqueta and Villamayor de Monjardín, ~675 m up, with the ruins of the castle of San Esteban de Deyo on the hill above.
After Villamayor, Spanish Wikipedia's table lists only one small place before Los Arcos, ~13 km on, so fill your bottle there.
Day 7: Los Arcos to Logroño (~28 km)

The longest day of the week. Sansol and Torres del Río face each other across a river, and Torres del Río has an octagonal Romanesque church, linked with the Templars. Viana, ~10 km short of Logroño, is a common place to split the day; Wikipedia says Cesare Borgia is buried there.
Between Viana and Logroño you leave Navarre for La Rioja. Logroño, on the Ebro, is the capital of La Rioja and a centre of the Rioja wine trade.
The character of these days
La Rioja is small, and the Camino crosses it in three days, between Logroño and the border with Castilla y León. It is a wine country. Rioja became in 1991 Spain's first
denominación de origen calificada

(DOCa), a quality designation for wine, according to Wikipedia, and its grapes grow in La Rioja, Navarre and the Basque province of Álava. The country between Logroño and Santo Domingo is low and rolling, with vines and small towns. The two Wikipedia tables used in this book agree to within a kilometre on all three days.
Day 8: Logroño to Nájera (~29 km)
A long day over low hills, from ~385 m at Logroño up to ~640 m near Ventosa and down to Nájera, at ~490 m. Navarrete, ~13 km along, is a natural place to split it.

Nájera is on the Najerilla river. It was once the capital of the Kingdom of Nájera-Pamplona, until Castile conquered it in 1054. The church of Santa María la Real was founded in 1052 by King García Sánchez III and is the burial place of kings of Navarre. Look in the app for when it can be visited.
Day 9: Nájera to Santo Domingo de la Calzada (~21 km)

A short day by way of Azofra and Cirueña, the highest point at ~755 m, then down to Santo Domingo, at ~640 m. From Azofra a variant leads towards the monastery of San Millán de la Cogolla; check before you go if it interests you.

Santo Domingo de la Calzada is named for Saint Dominic, who died in 1109 and helped pilgrims on the road. In its cathedral a pair of hens is kept at all times in the choir loft, descendants of the chickens of a legend: according to Wikipedia, two cooked, beheaded chickens came back to life to clear a pilgrim who had been wrongly accused of theft.
Day 10: Santo Domingo de la Calzada to Belorado (~23 km)

The road climbs by way of Grañón, ~725 m, to a high point near ~845 m, and drops towards Belorado, at ~770 m. Near Redecilla del Camino you pass from La Rioja into the province of Burgos, and so into Castilla y León.
Belorado is the first town of a new region, and ~130 m higher than Santo Domingo. The plateau is ahead of you, so fill your bottle.
The character of these days

The Meseta is the high plateau of central Spain, and the Camino crosses it at ~800 to ~900 m, from Burgos to León, mostly through farmland. The days are not steep. What they ask is patience, a hat, water and a plan for the long stretches between villages. Burgos, at the start, and León, at the end, are the cities that bracket it.
Distances are rounded, from Wikipedia's example itinerary and the table in Spanish Wikipedia. Where they differ by more than a couple of kilometres, the day says so.
Day 11: Belorado to San Juan de Ortega (~24 km)
A quiet day through Tosantos, Villambistia and Espinosa del Camino to Villafranca Montes de Oca, then a climb through the Montes de Oca, to ~1,000 m. Sources give this stage as ~21 to ~24 km.

San Juan de Ortega is a Romanesque monastery in the hamlet of Barrios de Colina, commonly thought to have been built around 1142 by Saint John of Ortega himself. Each March and September, Wikipedia says, a small window lets a beam of light fall on a sculpture of the Annunciation at 5 pm solar time.
Day 12: San Juan de Ortega to Burgos (~28 km)

You pass Agés and Atapuerca, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2000, where finds at the Gran Dolina date from about 800,000 years ago, the oldest known evidence of hominid settlement in Western Europe, says Wikipedia. Then come Cardeñuela Riopico, Orbaneja Riopico and Villafría, and the last ~10 km into the city, ~865 m up. Spanish Wikipedia's table puts this stage at ~31 km.
Burgos Cathedral, begun in 1221 in the French Gothic style, has been a World Heritage Site since 1984 and holds a tomb of El Cid. Burgos is a good city for a rest day.
Day 13: Burgos to Hornillos del Camino (~20 km)

A short first day on the plateau. You leave Burgos by Villalbilla de Burgos and Tardajos and cross to Rabé de las Calzadas and Hornillos del Camino, at ~850 to ~890 m up. Start early in summer, and carry a hat and water.
Day 14: Hornillos del Camino to Castrojeriz (~20 km)

By way of San Bol and Hontanas, ~11 km along, to the ruins of the Convent of San Antón, ~18 km along, where an arch still stands. Alfonso VII founded the convent in 1146 for the Order of St Anthony, whose brothers cared for pilgrims suffering from St Anthony's fire.
Castrojeriz is a single long street: the Camino runs through the town for ~1,500 m or more, past the ruins of a castle and the church of San Juan.
Day 15: Castrojeriz to Frómista (~23 km)

The road crosses the Pisuerga at Puente Fitero, ~10 km from Castrojeriz, and with it the line between the provinces of Burgos and Palencia. Itero de la Vega and Boadilla del Camino (~19 km) come before Frómista. Spanish Wikipedia's table gives ~25 km for the whole day.
Frómista's church of San Martín de Tours is a Romanesque church of the 11th century, built, Wikipedia says, partly with money from the widow of Sancho el Mayor of Navarre.
Day 16: Frómista to Carrión de los Condes (~19 km)

A short day through Población de Campos, Revenga de Campos, Villarmentero de Campos and Villalcázar de Sirga, where in the Middle Ages the church of the Virgin of Villasirga was an important point on the road.
Carrión de los Condes had a pilgrims' hospital, the Hospital de la Herrada, from 1209. Buy food and water here for tomorrow.
Day 17: Carrión de los Condes to Terradillos de los Templarios (~27 km)

You leave Carrión by the monastery of San Zoilo. Then comes ~17 to ~18 km with no village at all, to Calzadilla de la Cueza, so carry food and ample water, and do not start late. Ledigos and Terradillos de los Templarios follow. Wikipedia's example itinerary splits the day at Calzadilla de la Cueza.
Day 18: Terradillos de los Templarios to Bercianos del Real Camino (~25 km)

Past Moratinos and San Nicolás del Real Camino, on to Sahagún, ~13 km along, in the province of León. Wikipedia says it is often considered the halfway point of the walk, and holds some of the earliest examples of Mudéjar architecture.

At Calzada del Coto the Camino divides. This book goes by Bercianos and El Burgo Ranero. The alternative follows the old Roman road, the Vía Trajana, by Calzadilla de los Hermanillos, and German Wikipedia has the two meeting again at Reliegos.
Day 19: Bercianos del Real Camino to Mansilla de las Mulas (~26 km)

A long day across open country by El Burgo Ranero and Reliegos, with a village every ~6 to ~13 km, so you can pause often: El Burgo Ranero is ~7 km from Bercianos, Reliegos ~20 km. Mansilla de las Mulas has a medieval bridge over the Esla river, which pilgrims cross on the way to León.
The character of these days

This is the part of the road with the biggest swing. It starts in the city of León, at ~840 m, crosses the plain to Astorga, climbs to the Cruz de Ferro, at ~1,500 m the highest point of the whole Camino Francés, and drops into El Bierzo, a country that Wikipedia says is surrounded by mountains on all sides and so remarkably isolated. Then it climbs again, to O Cebreiro, where Galicia begins.
Distances are rounded, from Wikipedia's example itinerary and Spanish Wikipedia's table. The days say where they differ by more than a couple of kilometres.
Day 20: Mansilla de las Mulas to León (~19 km)

By Puente Villarente, Arcahueja and Valdelafuente, across open country, and then into León. The city began as a Roman military camp, and after 910 it became the capital of the Kingdom of León. Its cathedral, begun in the 13th century, is a great work of French-influenced Gothic, with one of the largest collections of medieval stained glass in the world, says Wikipedia.
The Basilica of San Isidoro was rededicated in 1063, and the Casa Botines, by Antoni Gaudí, was built in 1891 and 1892. León deserves a rest day.
Day 21: León to Villadangos del Páramo (~24 km)

The way out of León runs through its suburbs, Trobajo del Camino and La Virgen del Camino, then by Valverde de la Virgen and San Miguel del Camino to Villadangos del Páramo. Spanish Wikipedia also lists an alternative by Villar de Mazarife to Hospital de Órbigo.
Day 22: Villadangos del Páramo to Astorga (~28 km)

By San Martín del Camino to Hospital de Órbigo, ~10 km along, which has a long medieval stone bridge, restored, and on ~17 km more by Villares de Órbigo, Santibáñez de Valdeiglesia and San Justo de la Vega to Astorga.

Astorga began as the Roman camp of Asturica Augusta and is the seat of one of Spain's oldest dioceses. Its Episcopal Palace, built between 1889 and 1913, is by Gaudí, one of only three of his buildings outside Catalonia.
Day 23: Astorga to Foncebadón (~26 km)

The climb begins. You walk through Murias de Rechivaldo, Santa Catalina de Somoza and El Ganso to Rabanal del Camino, ~20 km from Astorga, where Wikipedia's example itinerary stops for the day, and on to Foncebadón, at ~1,430 m. The road rises from ~870 m in Astorga, a gain of ~560 m.

Foncebadón flourished in the Middle Ages as a place of shelter for pilgrims. By the 1990s, Wikipedia says, only two people lived among its ruins; pilgrims have brought it back to life. Weather in the mountains can change quickly, so carry a waterproof layer.
Day 24: Foncebadón to Ponferrada (~27 km)

Early on you reach the Cruz de Ferro, an iron cross on a tall wooden pole, at ~1,500 m. By tradition, pilgrims leave a stone carried from home at its foot; accounts of the tradition's origin vary, and it is better treated as a custom than as history. Manjarín (~4 km from Foncebadón), El Acebo (~11 km) and Riego de Ambrós follow, then Molinaseca (~19 km), at ~580 m, whose name comes from old mills on the Meruelo river.

The thing to watch is the descent: ~850 m in ~19 km to Molinaseca, steep and long. Poles help, and so does time. Ponferrada is the capital of El Bierzo. Its castle dates from the Knights Templar, to whom the king gave the town in the 12th century (the year usually given is 1178), to protect pilgrims on the road.
Day 25: Ponferrada to Villafranca del Bierzo (~23 km)

A flatter day, between ~465 m and ~525 m, by Columbrianos, Fuentesnuevas, Camponaraya and Cacabelos. Villafranca's name means "French town": in 1070, under Alfonso VI, a Cluniac monastery was founded there, and a community of French pilgrims grew around it. The church of Santiago has a Door of Forgiveness, the Puerta del Perdón, where, by tradition, pilgrims too ill to continue could receive the same indulgences as in Santiago. Ask locally about when it is open.
Day 26: Villafranca del Bierzo to O Cebreiro (~30 km)

Up the Valcarce valley by Trabadelo, La Portela de Valcarce, Vega de Valcarce (~19 km from Villafranca), Ruitelán, Las Herrerías and La Faba, climbing from ~505 m to ~1,300 m, a net gain of ~800 m. It is a long day, and Wikipedia's example itinerary splits it at La Faba, ~25 km from Villafranca.
O Cebreiro is a village of prehistoric origin, says the Xunta, between the mountain ranges of O Courel and Os Ancares. It keeps some
pallozas

, houses of an archaic type, and the church of Santa María la Real, built in 1965 to 1971 on the foundations of a pre-Romanesque church. A legend of a miracle of the Holy Grail clings to it. From here the Xunta measures ~155 km to Santiago.
The character of these days

Galicia begins at O Cebreiro, and from there the Xunta de Galicia measures ~155 km to Santiago by the San Xil route, or ~162 km by Samos. The country is greener and wetter than anything behind you, with small hamlets, oak woods and eucalyptus, and place names in Galician, many with the article
O
or
A
in front (O Cebreiro, A Calzada, A Salceda). Santiago receives ~1,500 mm of rain a year, so carry a waterproof whatever the month.

From Sarria on you walk with many other people: about 65 per cent of those who walked the French Way in 2024 started there. Distances in this chapter come from the Xunta's stage pages, which give a difficulty rating and an estimated time for each stage. Some other tables differ by up to ~4 km, and the days say where.
Day 27: O Cebreiro to Triacastela (~22 km)

The Xunta rates this stage "Medium-High" and gives ~22.2 km. From ~1,300 m the Way passes Liñares, Hospital da Condesa, the Alto do Poio, at ~1,330 m, Fonfría and O Biduedo, and drops to Triacastela, at ~665 m, a descent of ~635 m. It is mostly downhill and still hard on knees, so go slowly.
Day 28: Triacastela to Sarria (~18 km)

Here the Way divides. The shorter route by San Xil is ~18 km, rated "Medium-Low" by the Xunta, through small hamlets such as A Balsa, Montán, Pintín and Calvor. The route by Samos is ~25 km, also "Medium-Low", by San Cristovo do Real and the Monastery of Samos, which the Xunta calls one of the oldest monasteries in the western world, from the 6th century. King Alfonso II, who backed the first church over the tomb, was brought up there.
Sarria is, according to Wikipedia, ~115 km from the cathedral. It has the 13th-century church of O Salvador and the Convent of A Madalena, founded in the early 13th century as a pilgrims' hospital.
Day 29: Sarria to Portomarín (~22 km)

The Way leaves Sarria by the bridge of A Áspera and goes towards Barbadelo, ~4 km on, where the church of Santiago can be visited. The Xunta rates the day "Medium-High", and warns that after about a kilometre beside the railway there is the hardest hill of the stage. Then comes oak and meadow country, and the bridge over the Miño into Portomarín.
Portomarín was moved. The Belesar reservoir flooded the old town in the 1960s, and its main buildings, including the church of San Xoán, were rebuilt on higher ground.
Day 30: Portomarín to Palas de Rei (~25 km)

You cross the reservoir by a footbridge and climb steeply to Gonzar, ~8 km on. The Xunta rates that stretch "Medium-High", and the whole stage "Medium". Then comes Castromaior and Ligonde, whose hospital received the Emperor Charles I and his son Philip II, the best-known pilgrims of the 16th century, and so to Palas de Rei, a name that the Xunta says comes from a supposed royal palace.
Day 31: Palas de Rei to Arzúa (~29 km)

The longest day of the last week. The Xunta gives ~14.6 km to Melide and ~14.5 km on to Arzúa, while Wikipedia's example itinerary has the whole day as ~25 km. From Palas the Way goes through leafy woods by San Xiao do Camiño and O Leboreiro to Melide, where the Camino Primitivo joins. Melide is known for
polbo á feira
, Galician octopus.

From Melide the path is "easy to walk on", says the Xunta, with gradual climbs and descents, through Boente and Castañeda to Arzúa, where the Camino del Norte joins. Arzúa gives its name to a cheese with protected designation of origin.
Day 32: Arzúa to O Pedrouzo (~18 km)

A gentle day. The Xunta rates it "Low", and gives ~18.4 km, through meadows and woods of oak and eucalyptus, with hamlets such as A Calzada, A Salceda, A Brea and Santa Irene. The warning is the road: in the first half the Way follows stretches of the N-547 highway and crosses it several times, so watch for vehicles.
O Pedrouzo, also written Arca, is in the municipality of O Pino, the last before Santiago. It is tempting to push on tonight. Stay, and arrive fresh tomorrow.
Day 33: O Pedrouzo to Santiago de Compostela (~20 km)

The Xunta gives ~20.2 km for the last day, and Wikipedia's example itinerary ~16.5 km. After Santo Antón you climb to the municipality of Santiago, by O Amenal and San Paio, with Lavacolla about halfway.

Monte do Gozo, the Hill of Joy, at ~370 m and ~4.5 km from the centre, is where pilgrims traditionally cheered at the first sight of the cathedral's spires. Then the old town, and the cathedral. The chapter on arriving says what to do next.
Albergue life
An
albergue
is a pilgrims' hostel: a dormitory with bunk beds, a shared bathroom and usually a place to wash your clothes. You show your credencial at the door, and the host, the
hospitalero

, stamps it and tells you the house rules. The Pilgrim's Office lists "access to hostels offered by the Christian hospitality of the Way" as the first practical use of the credencial, and says that hostels without subsidies are kept going by what pilgrims contribute. Leave a place cleaner than you found it, and give what you can.

Hostels differ from region to region, and from year to year. In Galicia the Xunta runs a network of public hostels, and its rules give a sense of the kind of house you will find. The places are occupied as pilgrims arrive, and people on foot have priority. The maximum stay is one night, except in cases of illness or force majeure. Lights go out in the evening, and you must leave early in the morning. Elsewhere, hostels run by parishes, associations, towns and private hosts have their own rules, and private hostels, hotels and guesthouses can often be booked ahead. Which places exist, and which are open this month, is for the CaminoPlus app and for local advice, and this book does not list them.
The etiquette of a dormitory is short and kind.

items.t: Arrive, claim a bed, shower, wash and hang out your clothes. The evening is for resting.
Keep your voice low after the lights go out, and do not rustle bags at night or before dawn. Pack your rucksack in the hall.
Use a head torch, not the main light. Silence your phone.
Keep your pack and shoes off the bed, and shoes where the house puts them.
Earplugs are a small comfort that goes a long way. Somebody will snore, and if it is you, apologise at breakfast.

spans.t: Bedbugs

are a risk in any shared bed anywhere. Check the seams of the mattress, keep your pack and clothes off the bed, and if you find bites, tell the host and wash and dry everything hot. It is not a reason to avoid hostels, only a reason to look before you lie down.
If you are ill, tired or sleeping badly, take a private room. It is not cheating. A good night is part of the walk.
Eating
Many places along the Way offer a
menú del peregrino

, a set meal for pilgrims. Ask what is on it, and what it costs, before you sit. A set meal is a good way to eat well on a long day and an easy way to try what the region cooks. If you do not eat meat, or have an allergy, learn the Spanish words for what you cannot eat and say them first.
The road passes through many food regions, and here are a few names to look for.

items.t: is wine country, as its Rioja designation says.
is known for its blood sausage,
, octopus cooked Galician style, which Wikipedia lists as typical of Melide, and the cheese of Arzúa and A Ulloa, which has a protected designation of origin.

spans.t: You do not need to eat all of it. Pick one local thing a day, and eat it without a screen.
Water matters as much. Fill your bottle in each town, and take food for the long stretches, above all on day 17, ~17 to ~18 km without a village.
Resting
The Francés is long, and it is easy to treat it as a race with the calendar. Resist that. A rest day is part of the walk, and Wikipedia's own estimate of a typical walk allows for one or two.

The natural places are the cities: Pamplona after the Pyrenees, Burgos before the Meseta and León before the mountains. They are big enough to fill a day, and each has something worth the time. A day in Santiago at the end is the other one, and the chapter on arriving says why.

On the road, listen to your body before your plan. Take the short days as short days. If something hurts in a way that grows rather than fades, stop, rest, and let a doctor look at it. You are not walking to prove anything.
Feet and knees

Your feet carry the walk. The Xunta de Galicia says to take special care of them: apply foot cream, wear seamless cotton socks and footwear that has been broken in, keep your backpack light, carry a small first-aid kit, avoid large meals and take short, regular breaks. Treat a hot spot when you feel it, not when it is a blister, and stop for ten minutes to do it.

Knees suffer on the descents, and the Francés has several: the last ~6 km into Zubiri, the drop from the Alto del Perdón, the long way down from the Cruz de Ferro to Molinaseca, and the descent from the Alto do Poio to Triacastela. Shorten your stride, keep your knees soft and use poles if you like them. If you can, stop early on those days.
Heat

On the Meseta the land is open and the sun is direct. The Xunta advises hats or caps against sunstroke, and sunscreen of high protection factor. Pamplona and Burgos have recorded ~42 °C and ~39 °C in July. In summer:

items.t: Start at first light, and finish by early afternoon.
Carry more water than you think you need, and drink before you are thirsty.
Plan the long stretches. Day 17 passes ~17 to ~18 km with no village.
If you feel dizzy, confused or sick, stop in the shade, drink, cool yourself and ask for help.

spans.t: Cold, rain and mountains

The weather changes with the height. The route over the Pyrenees is closed to walkers in winter, and the lower road by Valcarlos is the choice in bad weather. The Xunta notes that many stages are in mountains, at about a thousand metres above the sea. The Cruz de Ferro, at ~1,500 m, and O Cebreiro, at ~1,300 m, stand higher than the towns below them and are usually colder. In Galicia it rains in every season, and in autumn and winter heavily.

Carry a waterproof layer in every month, as the Xunta advises, and a cap for the cold in high places. If fog or storm closes in on a mountain stage, turn back to the last village, or wait, and do not push on to keep a schedule.
Roads, vehicles and the dark

Much of the way is on paths, but not all of it. The Xunta warns that on the way from Arzúa the road is crossed several times, and the Camino follows stretches of the N-547 highway. The Confraternity of St James says that a reflective vest is a legal requirement in Spain when you walk on roads in darkness or poor visibility, and a good idea in hunting season. Where there is no path, walk facing the traffic, and step off the road when a lorry is coming.
If a dog comes towards you, stay calm, do not run, and walk on.
When to stop

Stopping is part of the plan. Stop for pain that grows rather than fades, for a fever, for dizziness, or for anything that worries you, and see a doctor. A day or two lost to rest is cheaper than a month lost to injury. Tell someone your plan, and check that your insurance covers you in Spain.
In an emergency in Spain, as elsewhere in the European Union, call
. It is the European emergency number, and it connects you to the emergency services.
Why people walk

People walk the French Way for faith, for sport, for grief, for a pause between one chapter of life and the next, to see Spain at the speed of a person, or because they were asked to, and some cannot say why. All of those are real reasons, and none needs defending.

The road itself began as a Christian pilgrimage to the tomb of St James, and it still ends at his cathedral. The Pilgrim's Office, which issues the Compostela, says that its credencial is for pilgrims who walk with a Christian sentiment, "even if it is only with an attitude of search". The Xunta de Galicia describes the pilgrimage today as spiritual and ecumenical, and open to knowledge, friendship and mutual understanding. You can walk in that spirit without sharing the faith, and the road asks only that you walk with respect for the people who do.
What a month of walking is for

The Francés has room built into it. You cross five regions, each with its own landscape. The days are long enough for thoughts to run their course, and the evenings are for company or for quiet. The Xunta writes that, for the medieval mind, the pilgrim was sent from heaven and was to be treated as Christ himself, and that the road's hospitals grew from that idea. You are, in the oldest sense of the word, a guest. Arrive tired, grateful and polite.

At the Cruz de Ferro, ~1,500 m up, pilgrims leave a stone brought from home, a custom with disputed origins, often described as a way of letting go of a worry or a loss. You do not need to carry one. But it is worth asking, before you leave, what you would put down if you could.
Questions for the walk
Take one a day, or none.

items.t: What are you carrying that you could leave on the road?
What did you notice today that you would have missed in a car?
Who walked with you today, in the flesh or in your mind?
What does your body need that you have been ignoring?
What will you be glad to have done by the time you reach Santiago?

spans.t: Walking alone, walking together

The Francés can be walked alone and in company, sometimes in the same hour. Greet the people you pass. Let a silence be a silence. If you want to be alone, say so kindly, and if someone else does, respect it. A friendship made on the road may last for years or for an afternoon, and both belong to it.
The last kilometres

The way into Santiago passes Monte do Gozo, the Hill of Joy, at ~370 m and ~4.5 km from the centre, where pilgrims have traditionally cheered at the first sight of the cathedral's spires. Then you walk down into the city and on to the old town. If you can, arrive early in the day, with your credencial in a pocket you can reach.
The cathedral

The French Way ends where every Way ends: at the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, built over the reputed tomb of St James. Wikipedia dates the start of the present building to 1075. It is Romanesque at its core, with Gothic and Baroque additions. The Pórtico da Gloria, the carved Romanesque doorway inside, is a work of Master Mateo, dated to 1188, and the Baroque façade facing the Praza do Obradoiro was completed in 1740. The Xunta de Galicia records that the apostle's remains were hidden in 1589 for fear of an English attack and found again in 1879.
The cathedral has a Holy Door, opened only in a Holy Year, and the next is 2027. Take a moment in the square before you do anything else. Sit on the stones if you wish.
The Pilgrim's Office and the Compostela

The Pilgrim's Office in Santiago issues the Compostela. The chapter on where to start gives the rule in the Office's words: the certificate is for those who come to the tomb of the Apostle for religious and/or spiritual reasons, and who have done at least the last hundred kilometres on foot or on horseback, or the last two hundred by bicycle, shown by the credencial, stamped along the route. If your walk was close to the limit, or unusual, ask the Office, which decides.

The Office awards the Compostela to those who walk for religious or spiritual reasons, and it describes the pilgrimage it has in mind as one made "with a Christian sentiment, even if it is only with an attitude of search". If that does not describe your reason for walking, ask the Pilgrim's Office what it can give you: it also offers a Certificate of Distance, which records the kilometres you walked from wherever you started.

Bring your credencial, stamped with the date and the place in each box. You collect a ticket with a QR code, which lets you follow your place in the queue. The Office says that in times of great influx it cannot guarantee that you will receive the Compostela the same day. Allow for that in August and in a Holy Year. The Office says that its reception service and the issue of the Compostela carry no charge. Its website gives its address and its current opening hours, which are not in this book because they change.

If you walked for other reasons, or are not sure your reasons count, the Office also offers a separate certificate of distance, whatever your starting point. It records the day and starting point, the kilometres covered, the day of arrival and the route. It is sold, and the Office states the price.
The pilgrims' Mass

The Xunta says that a pilgrims' Mass is held at the cathedral's high altar every day. At its start a list is read of the pilgrims who arrived in the last 24 hours, with their starting points and their nationalities or home provinces. In Holy Years there are more Masses, because of the crowds, and the Xunta advises arriving well ahead. Check the cathedral's own website for the times.
The botafumeiro, the great swinging censer, is used at Masses on key dates, and on other occasions on request from pilgrim groups. Do not count on seeing it.
The next day

Do not leave the morning after you arrive. A day in Santiago lets the walk settle. Wash your clothes, sleep late and look at the old town. You may like to see the building on the Praza do Obradoiro that the Catholic Monarchs founded in the 16th century as the Royal Hospital for pilgrims, and which has been a hotel since 1954, according to the Pilgrim's Office.

If you still have legs and time, you can walk on to the coast. In the CaminoPlus catalog the walk from Santiago to Finisterre and Muxía is ~90 km. The Confraternity of St James notes that Finisterre was once believed to be the end of the world, which is where its name comes from.
The second stage

The walk ends in Santiago, and going home is the next stage. The routine you left is waiting where you left it, and you have changed a little, so give yourself some days before everything starts again at full speed.

Write down what you want to keep while it is clear: a few lines about the days that mattered, the people, the questions you carried. If you kept a journal in the CaminoPlus app, read it a week after you are home. It is easier to see a month once it is behind you.
If the walk was tied to something, such as a loss, a decision or a change of work, give that part of your life its own time as well. The road has done its share, and the rest is yours to carry on.
Keeping the Way alive

Walking is the habit to keep. An hour on foot each day costs little, and it keeps the legs and the quiet that the road gave you. Keep in touch with the people you met, and consider the associations of friends of the Camino, whose founding in the 1950s and 1960s, the Xunta says, began the road's revival.
Walking again

You may want to go back to the road, to the same Camino or to another. The French Way is one of 14 routes in the CaminoPlus catalog, from the sea to the mountains. The English Way, the Portuguese Way and the walk to Finisterre and Muxía are shorter, and the Northern Way is ~820 km. You do not have to decide yet.
Buen Camino
, again and always.
With the CaminoPlus app
CaminoPlus
is the offline-first companion app for the Camino de Santiago, with maps that work without signal, stays and cafes, a pilgrim passport with stamps, a journal and friends. The paid plan is called
Pilgrim Plus
. The app is still in development, so look in the app for what is available on the French Way today, and use it, not this book, for beds, cafes, closures and weather.

A reminder about the passport: the Pilgrim's Office asks for the stamped credencial. A passport in CaminoPlus, or in any app other than the Office's own digital credential, is a keepsake until the Office says otherwise.

Thanks go to the people who keep the Way: the associations of friends of the Camino, the hosts who open the hostels, and the people in the towns and villages who point the way and say
Buen Camino
